content: 1. The system is designed to maintain pressure at a minimum set level. The number of operational cycles is counted, and the apparatus automatically shuts off after completing the predetermined number of cycles. If the maximum pressure is not achieved within a specified time frame or if the pressure drops beyond the permissible limit during the hold time, this indicates a potential leak. In such cases, the system triggers an audio alarm and shuts down. 2. The tank drop test for compression sprayers evaluates whether the sprayer can continue to function effectively after being accidentally dropped from the operator's back. The tank, pressurized to the maximum recommended level and filled with water to its maximum operational volume, is dropped from a height of 60 cm onto a flat wooden surface (20–30 mm thick and 800 mm square) placed on a level floor. A metal cage surrounds the setup to protect the tester from injury. The test involves six upright drops and six drops tilted at a 10° angle to simulate how the tank hangs on the shoulder. After the test, the sprayer must function normally and meet leakage test requirements. 3. The strap drop test involves filling the sprayer tank to its recommended maximum level with water. The entire sprayer is suspended by its straps and lifted 30 cm above a solid horizontal support (a 75 mm diameter pole) before being allowed to drop freely and hang by the straps. This test is repeated 25 times. The straps and their fittings must not sustain any damage during the test. 4. The tank fatigue test for a compression sprayer uses a computerized system to simulate prolonged use. The system applies repeated pressure cycles to the tank to assess its durability under operational conditions. 5. The strap absorbency test involves removing the straps and any padding from the sprayer and weighing them when dry. The straps are then fully immersed in water for 2 minutes. After removal, excess liquid is shaken off, and the straps are hung freely to drain for 10 minutes before being re-weighed. The weight increase after immersion should not exceed 10% of the dry weight. In humid conditions, the straps may need to dry overnight (8+ hours) before re-weighing. 6. The trigger valve durability test involves mounting the valve on a test rig designed to open and close the valve at a rate of 10–15 cycles per minute using a cam mechanism. The test applies less than 500 kPa to the valve face, with a suspension of 20 g/L silica in water flowing at 75 L/min at 300 kPa to test the abrasion resistance of the valve components. The nozzle discharges liquid into a reservoir, which recirculates the liquid under pressure to the valve inlet. The test suspension is replaced every 8 hours. After an initial test of 500 cycles at 100 kPa, the test continues for 50,000 cycles at 300 kPa and concludes with 500 cycles at 1000 kPa. A pneumatically controlled test apparatus may also be used, and the system shuts down if the valve fails. 7. The spray output test for compression and other hydraulic sprayers involves using an electrically operated solenoid valve to control water flow from the sprayer for exactly one minute. The water is collected in a measuring cylinder or pre-weighed beaker to determine the nozzle output by weight. 8. The spray pattern test evaluates the nozzle's spray distribution according to ISO 5682-1:2017. The nozzle is mounted centrally 450 mm above an inclined patternator with channels (ideally 25 mm wide) to collect liquid across the spray swath. Tubes at the lower edge of each channel collect the liquid for analysis. 9. For mist blowers, the flow rate is measured with the engine operating at optimal speed. The liquid output in a high-velocity air stream is determined by filling the spray tank to the 10 L mark and recording the time it takes for the liquid level to decrease to 5 L. Measurements must be taken when the liquid level is horizontal in the sprayer. 10. For cold foggers, the fogger is started, and the engine speed is adjusted to establish proper insecticide tank pressure. The discharge tube is removed from the nozzle and held at the same level. The control valve is activated to start discharge, and the flow is collected in a spare cylinder for one minute to measure the flow rate in mL/min. 11. For thermal foggers, a similar technique is used as for cold foggers. After ensuring liquid is in the line between the pesticide tank and nozzle, a known volume is added to the tank, and the machine is run until the tank is empty. The volume required to refill and the runtime determine the flow rate. 12. The nozzle test for droplet size uses a recognized non-intrusive laser system connected to a computer for data display. The nozzle directs spray through the laser beam, and the droplet size spectrum is measured. The system can measure droplet sizes from 5 µm to 2000 µm and can operate in a sweep mode for continuous measurements. Data is processed and exported to an Excel spreadsheet. 13. The sprayer durability test for lever-operated knapsack sprayers involves mounting the sprayer, filled with water, on a rig that simulates being carried on a user's back. The lever is linked to a mechanism powered by an electric motor to operate at up to 30 strokes per minute. The test is conducted for a minimum of 250 hours. 14. The output of hydraulic nozzles used on sprayers can change after use, especially when water contains small sand particles that erode the nozzle orifice. Operators should regularly calibrate nozzle output by collecting spray in a measuring cylinder or jug for one minute. If the output increases by more than 10%, the nozzle should be replaced to avoid excessive discharge and potential overdosing of insecticide. Spray distribution should also be checked by spraying a dry surface with water and observing the wetting pattern. 15. Electrically powered knapsack sprayers are now commercially available but have not yet been evaluated for indoor residual spraying. These sprayers eliminate the need for manual pumping and can be used for wall surface spraying and larvicide application. They must include features such as a filter to prevent nozzle blockage, a battery protected from pesticides, and a battery management system to prevent overcharging and overheating. The battery should ideally recharge fully within 4 hours, and an indicator for battery power level is recommended.
